title: Miri and piri as thought
hookLine: spiritual and worldly life held together, not split

cards: Two swords, worn at once. That's how Sikh tradition remembers Guru Hargobind on the day he took up the guruship: one sword at each side. You met him and his two swords in year one.
When people asked why, the answer came in a pair of words: one sword for miri, one for piri.
It's easy to live as if life comes in two drawers: one for the job, the rent, the news, who does the dishes; another, smaller, for prayer or quiet. Today is about refusing the two drawers.
Not the swords themselves, but the thought behind them.

teach.h: MIRI: THE WORLD. PIRI: THE SPIRIT.
teach.b: Miri is worldly authority: the life of rule, justice, work, the public square. Piri is spiritual authority: the life of prayer, the Word, the inner path.
Alongside the two swords, tradition says Guru Hargobind raised the Akal Takht, a seat of worldly authority, facing the Harmandir, the house of prayer. Two buildings, looking at each other.
Not one behind the other, not one in another city. Facing. The idea didn't start with the swords.
Guru Arjan, in the var in Raag Gujri, says it with ordinary words.
In paraphrase: meeting the true Guru, a person finds the complete way, and is set free while laughing, playing, dressing and eating. Notice the verbs. Laughing.
Liberation isn't kept in a separate room for special occasions. It happens in the middle of the ordinary. So what does the thought ask?

teach.h: PRAYER AT WORK; WORK AS PRAYER.
teach.b: If miri and piri belong together, prayer has to show up at work, and work has to be done as if the Guru were watching.

Sikh teachers read the two swords as a call to care about justice as a spiritual duty, and to keep the inner life awake while doing it. A prayer that never touches how you treat people stays in the drawer.
A public life with no inner life loses its way. The thought refuses both.

how: Sikhs speak of miri and piri, worldly and spiritual authority, as held together, remembered in Guru Hargobind's two swords and in the Akal Takht facing the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar.

games.q: what does “miri and piri as thought” mean?
o: two rival leaders, one for war and one for prayer
two holy days, one for work and one for rest
worldly and spiritual life held together, not split

games.q: two swords, one life: tap the pairs.

s: miri and piri means keeping prayer and work in separate parts of life
it means holding them together, not split.
Guru Arjan speaks of liberation while laughing, playing, dressing and eating
in the var in Raag Gujri, in paraphrase.
tradition says the Akal Takht was built in a different city from the Harmandir
tradition says it was raised facing the Harmandir.

games.q: you're the new Guru, and you want to show that the spiritual and the worldly belong together. tradition says you do what?
o: wear one sword and leave prayer to others.
give up all worldly power and retreat to pray.
wear two swords, one for miri and one for piri.
games.why: Sikh tradition remembers Guru Hargobind wearing two swords, and raising the Akal Takht facing the Harmandir.

practice: Picture the next ordinary task you'll do, dishes, an email, a drive, a diaper, a spreadsheet, and see yourself doing it.
Without changing the task at all, carry this same breath and quiet into it, with Waheguru in the back of your mind if you pray. Same task, no drawer at all.

wordCard.voice: Miri and piri as thought. Worldly life and spiritual life held together, not split: two swords, two buildings facing, one life. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: miri and piri, worldly and spiritual authority.

carryVoice: Your line: both together. Two swords, one life. I'll be here tomorrow.
